q: In a medallion architecture, what belongs in the bronze layer?
options: Only the rows that passed validation
why: Bronze is the untouched copy. Keeping it lets you rebuild silver and gold after fixing a bug.

q: A row fails validation (negative units). What is good practice?
options: Move it to a quarantine table with the reason, and keep the pipeline running
why: Quarantine keeps good data flowing and keeps the bad rows, with reasons, so they can be reviewed and fixed at the source.

q: What does it mean that a pipeline is idempotent?
options: Running it twice gives the same result as running it once
It only runs once per day
why: Re-runs after a failure must not create duplicates. Idempotency is what makes retries safe.

q: RPO (recovery point objective) is:
options: How much recent work you can afford to lose, measured in time
why: If you back up daily, your RPO is up to 24 hours of changes. RTO is the separate question of how long a restore takes.

q: A backup you have never restored is:
options: Unproven: only a successful test restore shows it works
Automatically verified by the file size
why: Files can be empty, truncated or corrupt. A restore drill turns a hope into evidence.

q: Data lineage answers:
options: Where a number came from and what depends on it
why: Lineage lets you trace a wrong number back to its source and see what breaks if you change a column.

q: A pipeline run finishes without an error. What should you still check?
options: Nothing; no error means it worked
That the row counts in and out make sense
The name of the output file
why: A run can succeed technically and still lose or duplicate rows. Counts are the quickest check.

q: Where should you import your own business data?
options: Into Practice, next to the sample data
Into the Real workspace, kept apart from Practice
Into any workspace; they are the same
why: Practice and Real are separate databases so sample data and real data never mix.

q: Your health baseline lists 'no backups'. What is the right response?
options: Treat it as a priority: set up a backup and test a restore
Delete old data to reduce risk
why: No backup means one failure loses everything. A backup counts only once you have restored from it.

q: A query is slow. What do you do first?
options: Measure it and read the query plan to see where the time goes
why: Optimising without measuring wastes effort and can make things worse. The plan shows where the time is spent.

q: What does a checkpoint do for a DuckDB database?
options: Writes the write-ahead log into the main database file, keeping the log small
Copies the database to a backup
why: Changes are first written to the write-ahead log. A checkpoint merges them into the database file, so the log does not keep growing.

q: Where should designing a data flow start?
options: With the business need, then sources, storage, organising and delivery
why: Tools come last. The need decides which data, storage and delivery you require.

q: Which store suits large amounts of raw, mixed-format files you may want later?
why: A lake keeps raw data in its original form cheaply. A warehouse holds cleaned, modelled data for reporting.

q: What do you decide first when designing a star schema?
options: The grain: what one fact row means
why: Facts, measures and dimensions all follow from the grain. Without it, joins and totals give wrong answers.

q: What should a warehouse load do after it finishes?
options: Reconcile counts and totals back to the source
why: A warehouse is only as good as its last load. Reconciling to the source shows whether anything was lost or doubled.

q: What makes a data management plan useful?
options: Every rule has an accountable owner and the plan has a review date
why: Rules nobody owns are not followed, and a plan without a review date goes stale.

q: Which four words describe analytics-ready data?
why: The data engineer's job is data that is accurate, reliable, compliant with the rules that govern it, and available when consumers need it.

q: Which kind of metadata says what a column means and who owns it?
why: Technical metadata describes structures, process metadata describes what ran, and business metadata gives meaning and ownership.

q: What is the difference between ETL and ELT?
options: ETL is faster in every case
ETL transforms before loading; ELT loads raw data first and transforms it in the destination
They are two names for the same thing
why: The order of Transform and Load differs. ELT suits destinations that can transform data at scale.

q: What is a wrangling log for?
options: Recording every change so the result can be explained and repeated
why: Changing data without recording it makes results impossible to explain or reproduce.

q: At which levels should data security be reviewed?
options: Physical, network, application and data, plus monitoring
why: A weakness at any level, including backup copies, can expose the data.

q: What is the right order when tuning performance?
options: Measure, change one thing, measure again
Change one thing and do not measure
why: Changing one thing at a time, with a before and after measurement, shows what actually helped.

q: You rely on an average order value. What else should you check?
options: Nothing; an average says it all
The spread and outliers, since an average can hide them
why: Two very different sets of values can share an average. Spread and outliers show whether the average is representative.

q: How should compliance be treated across the data lifecycle?
options: Ongoing: a written basis and an owner for every stage, and a retention rule for personal data
why: Rules apply at every stage, and they change. Each stage needs a basis and someone responsible.

q: What does DataOps add to delivering data changes?
options: Small iterations with automated tests and metrics
why: Automated tests and metrics make each small change safe to ship and easy to improve.

q: A table's readiness score is low. What do you do?
options: Find and fix the cause behind the score
why: The score is a symptom. Chasing the number without fixing the cause does not make the data better.

q: A book can have many authors. How should this be stored?
options: A comma-separated list in one column
A link table with one row per book and author
why: A link table makes each pairing a row that can be keyed, joined and checked. A list in one column cannot be.

q: To find what changed between two snapshots you need what?
options: A unique key to match rows between the two snapshots
why: Without a unique key you cannot tell whether a row changed, is new, or was removed.

q: Users report a wrong number in a report. Where should the fix be made?
options: At the source of the problem, so every report is right
why: Fixing the report hides the problem and leaves the same error in every other place that uses the data.

q: After reviewing the whole data ecosystem, what should you improve first?
why: The system is only as strong as its weakest link, whether that is sources, storage, organising or delivery.

q: Why give every table an owner and a class?
options: So someone is accountable and the right controls apply
It is needed to import data
why: Unowned data is nobody's problem until it breaks. The class decides what protection it needs.

q: A scan finds no personal-data columns. What is the right reading?
options: It found none it recognises; review the columns yourself, since scans miss things
why: Pattern scans miss unusual names and formats. Treat the result as a help, not a guarantee.

q: Does a high score on the controls checklist certify compliance?
options: No; it is evidence that data is handled on purpose
why: The checklist helps you see gaps. Compliance is decided against the actual rules that apply to you.

q: In a dbt-style project, what decides the order models are built?
why: ref() declares which model a SELECT reads, so the tool builds the dependencies first.

q: A1 reads B1 and B1 reads A1. The sheet has...
options: A circular reference with no answer
why: Each cell needs the other first, so there is no valid calculation order.

q: A topic has 3 partitions and a consumer group has 5 members. How many members get work?
why: A partition goes to one member of the group at a time, so extra members sit idle.

q: A cron line sets both day-of-month 13 and day-of-week Friday. It runs...
options: On the 13th and on every Friday
why: In standard cron, when both fields are restricted either one matching is enough.
